question:
Patient note:
A 28-year-old man who works as a freelance graphic animator presented to the combined pulmonary–infectious-disease clinic late this afternoon for an interval assessment of his chronic respiratory symptoms and review of his antiretroviral regimen before a five-week assignment in Singapore that will involve frequent overnight editing sessions in air-conditioned studios. He was diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus infection at age 24 during evaluation of prolonged mononucleosis-like illness; baseline studies at that time revealed an absolute CD4 lymphocyte count of 108 cells/µL, an HIV-1 RNA level exceeding 400 000 copies/mL, and oropharyngeal candidiasis that resolved with fluconazole. A once-daily combination of bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide was initiated within two weeks of diagnosis, and pharmacy refill records confirm uninterrupted adherence. The most recent laboratory panel drawn two weeks ago demonstrated an undetectable viral load and a CD4 recovery to 278 cells/µL, yet he remains enrolled in statewide Ryan White services and continues daily trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis because his count is still below the 200–cell threshold at which it was originally started. He reports no episodes of Kaposi sarcoma lesions, cryptococcal meningitis, cytomegalovirus retinitis, toxoplasmic encephalitis, or recurrent bacterial pneumonias; vaccinations are current, including the 20-valent conjugate pneumococcal formulation administered last autumn. Pulmonary history antedates his HIV diagnosis: childhood atopic asthma progressed during late adolescence when he began smoking clove cigarettes at concerts, ultimately accumulating an estimated eight pack-years before quitting two years ago after an emergency-department visit for wheezing. Office spirometry performed last month showed an FEV1 of 2.1 L (65 % predicted) with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.59 and less than 8 % bronchodilator reversibility, consistent with partially fixed obstruction attributable to chronic airway remodeling; diffusion capacity was 72 % of predicted. His maintenance therapy consists of budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 µg two inhalations twice daily and tiotropium 18 µg every morning, with albuterol used three or four times per week during brisk walks to a city subway station. The last oral glucocorticoid burst occurred six months ago after an influenza B infection, and he has never required intubation or admission to an intensive-care unit. Exercise tolerance presently encompasses climbing four flights to his loft while carrying groceries, although he pauses at the top to catch his breath; he denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, exertional chest pressure, palpitations, or syncope. Digestive review is significant for a history of chronic hepatitis B discovered on screening serologies obtained at HIV diagnosis; hepatitis B surface antigen remains positive, e antigen is negative, HBV DNA last month was 2 400 IU/mL, alanine aminotransferase measured 54 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 48 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. An abdominal ultrasound performed eight weeks ago depicted a mildly enlarged, homogeneous liver with smooth contour, no focal masses, and patent portal as well as hepatic veins; there is no ascites, splenomegaly, or abdominal varices. He consumes no alcohol, follows a plant-forward diet, and avoids over-the-counter herbal supplements that might worsen transaminases. Endocrine history is unrevealing: a fasting plasma glucose drawn with his viral panel was 94 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c 5.2 %; he has never required dietary counseling for carbohydrate restriction or pharmacologic glycemic control. Renal function is normal with sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 11 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 118 mL/min/1.73 m²; urinalysis is bland. He has never experienced a myocardial infarction, angina requiring hospital evaluation, or undergone coronary revascularization; no cardiologist has ever diagnosed congestive heart failure, and his most recent transthoracic echocardiogram five months ago showed a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 60 % without wall-motion abnormalities. He has never suffered a transient ischemic attack or cerebrovascular accident, and neurologic examinations have never revealed hemiplegia or focal deficits. Outpatient neuropsychologic screening performed last year documented normal executive function without evidence of dementia. Complete blood counts drawn with each HIV monitoring panel have remained within normal reference ranges and show no cytopenias or blasts, and oncology records confirm he has never been evaluated for or treated for leukemia or lymphoma. Serum creatinine has remained below 1 mg/dL on all measurements, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate persistently above 90 mL/min/1.73 m², indicating the absence of chronic kidney disease. Upper-gastrointestinal endoscopy has never been required, and he has no history of diagnosed peptic ulcer disease or upper-tract bleeding. He denies abdominal pain, dyspepsia, hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, or prior endoscopic therapy for ulcers, takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and uses omeprazole only sporadically for occasional reflux after late-night spicy ramen. Neurologic review is negative for transient speech disturbance, focal weakness, numbness, facial droop, gait imbalance, seizures, or cognitive decline; he edits high-resolution video files for hours without lapses in concentration and manages complex rendering schedules on spreadsheet macros. Family pedigree reveals a mother with seasonal allergic rhinitis and a father who underwent coronary angiography for atypical chest pain at 60 that showed nonobstructive disease; no first-degree relatives developed stroke, dementia, dialysis-dependent kidney failure, or insulin-requiring diabetes. He abstains from recreational drugs, drinks coffee but no energy beverages, and limits himself to one craft beer per month; he has no tattoos and engages in consistent condom use with a long-term partner whose HIV status is negative on quarterly testing. Medications also include vitamin D3 2000 IU daily, cetirizine 10 mg at bedtime during pollen season, and a nicotine-free vape used intermittently for anxiety relief. He reports no medication allergies. Review of systems today is negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss exceeding five pounds, chronic cough beyond baseline, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, diarrhea, jaundice, pruritus, hematochezia, or skin rashes other than occasional eczematous patches in winter. Physical examination finds a lean man seated comfortably, speaking in full sentences without accessory-muscle use. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg in the right arm, pulse 78 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 96 % on ambient air, weight 70 kg, height 178 cm, body-mass index 22 kg/m². Conjunctivae are pink and sclerae anicteric; oral mucosa is moist without thrush. Cervical nodes are not enlarged, carotid upstrokes are brisk with no bruit, and jugular venous pulsation rises to 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45 °. The point of maximal impulse is at the fifth intercostal space mid-clavicular line; S1 and S2 are crisp with no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs reveal mild end-expiratory wheezes diffusely, prolonged expiration, but no crackles; percussion is resonant and fremitus symmetric. The abdomen is flat, soft, non-tender, with a liver edge palpable 1.5 cm below the right costal margin that is smooth and non-tender; there is no splenomegaly, shifting dullness, or fluid wave. Extremities are warm, without clubbing, cyanosis, or edema; toenail capillary refill is under two seconds. Neurologic examination shows an alert, oriented individual with fluent speech, intact cranial nerves II–XII, symmetric 5/5 strength, normal sensation to light touch and vibration, 2+ deep-tendon reflexes, and steady heel-to-toe gait. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained during the visit demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, axis within normal limits, no Q waves, and ST-T segments appropriate for age. Portable spirometry repeated in clinic corroborates the obstructive pattern seen previously with no significant reversibility after bronchodilator. He seeks guidance on inhaler technique adjustments for the humid equatorial climate, recommendations regarding booster immunizations prior to travel, and clarification on altitude precautions for a planned weekend hike up Mount Batur in Bali.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums weighted chronic conditions and age points.
- Age 28: younger than 50 → 0.
- AIDS: the historical CD4 count of 108 cells/µL meets the AIDS threshold of <200. Recovery to 278 on therapy does not erase that history → 6.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: symptomatic obstructive airway disease requiring maintenance inhalers, with FEV₁/FVC 0.59 → 1.
- Mild liver disease: chronic hepatitis B with preserved synthetic function and no evidence of portal hypertension → 1.
- No additional qualifying cardiac, peripheral vascular, cerebrovascular, neurologic, rheumatologic, ulcer, diabetic, renal, or malignant condition is documented → 0.
Sum: 0 + 6 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 8.
Final answer: 8
